atp.short: The molecule whose splitting (hydrolysis) to ADP and phosphate powers muscle contraction and ion pumps. The only energy currency muscle spends directly.

adp.short: What is left of ATP after one phosphate is split off. Rising ADP is a signal that drives ATP resynthesis.

hydrolysis.short: Splitting a molecule with water. ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi) releases the energy muscles use.

cross-bridge.short: The link a myosin head makes with actin. Each attach–pull–detach cycle splits one ATP and moves the filaments a few nanometres.

pcr.short: A high-energy phosphate store in muscle that rebuilds ATP almost instantly via creatine kinase. About three times the ATP store; mostly used within 10–30 s of an all-out effort.

creatine-kinase.short: The enzyme that moves a phosphate from PCr to ADP, making ATP (PCr + ADP + H⁺ ⇌ creatine + ATP). Runs both ways; in recovery it rebuilds PCr.

glycolysis.short: Breakdown of glucose or glycogen to pyruvate in the cytosol, making ATP fast without oxygen. Some pyruvate always becomes lactate; more does when it is made faster than the mitochondria take it up.

oxidative-phosphorylation.short: ATP made in mitochondria using oxygen, from carbohydrate and fat. Slowest maximal rate of the three routes, but almost unlimited capacity.

time-constant.short: For an exponential process, the time to get 63% of the way to the end. Half-time = τ × ln 2 ≈ 0.69 τ.

pyruvate.short: The three-carbon end product of glycolysis. Either enters the mitochondria to be fully oxidised, or is turned into lactate in the cytosol.

glycogen.short: The stored form of glucose: long branched chains kept in muscle and liver. Muscle glycogen is the main carbohydrate fuel in hard exercise.

nad.short: An electron carrier. Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle load it with electrons (NAD⁺ → NADH); the electron transport chain or lactate formation unloads it.

phosphofructokinase.short: The enzyme of the committed step of glycolysis and its main control point: sped up by rising AMP when ATP is being used fast, slowed by acidity.

lactate.short: Made from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase, which also regenerates NAD⁺. Formed all the time, more when glycolysis is fast; a fuel, not a waste product.

acidosis.short: A fall in pH (a rise in free H⁺) in muscle or blood. In hard exercise muscle pH falls by several tenths of a unit.

mitochondria.short: The structures in the cell where the Krebs cycle, beta-oxidation and the electron transport chain run, using oxygen to make most of the ATP.

acetyl-coa.short: A two-carbon unit carried by coenzyme A. Pyruvate and fatty acids both become acetyl-CoA, which feeds the Krebs cycle.

krebs-cycle.short: A loop of reactions in the mitochondria that breaks acetyl-CoA down to CO₂ and loads NAD⁺ and FAD with electrons.

electron-transport-chain.short: Protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane that pass electrons from NADH and FADH₂ to oxygen, pumping protons to drive ATP synthase.

p-o-ratio.short: ATP made per oxygen atom used: about 2.5 for electrons from NADH and 1.5 for electrons from FADH₂.

beta-oxidation.short: The pathway in the mitochondria that cuts fatty acids into two-carbon acetyl-CoA units, making one NADH and one FADH₂ per turn.

imtg.short: Fat stored as droplets inside muscle fibres, close to the mitochondria. A fuel alongside fatty acids delivered by the blood from adipose tissue.

carnitine-shuttle.short: The carrier system (CPT1 and CPT2) that moves long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria. A main brake on fat oxidation at high intensity.

fatmax.short: The exercise intensity at which fat oxidation per minute is highest, often around 45–65% of VO₂max; varies a lot between people.

oxygen-deficit.short: The gap between the oxygen an effort needs and the oxygen actually taken up, mostly at its start. PCr and glycolysis cover the gap.

epoc.short: Oxygen uptake above resting after exercise. Once called the oxygen debt; it has a fast and a slow component.

crossover-point.short: The power output above which energy from carbohydrate exceeds that from fat (Brooks and Mercier, 1994). Training moves it to higher power.

rer.short: CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ used, measured at the mouth. About 0.7 when burning only fat, 1.0 when burning only carbohydrate.

gross-efficiency.short: Mechanical power ÷ metabolic power. In cycling about 20%: the rest of the energy becomes heat.
